verses.1: Al-Mizan explains tabāruk as the abundant issuance of goodness and blessing. God’s having every kingdom in His hand is figurative for His complete dominion over all things and over whatever they possess, a formulation fuller than calling Him King or saying that the kingdom belongs to Him. His unlimited power necessarily accompanies this absolute kingdom: kingdom is an attribute of divine act (ṣifāt al-fiʿl), while power is an attribute of divine essence (ṣifāt al-dhāt). The verse consequently indicates the possibility of the resurrection subsequently discussed.
verses.2: Al-Mizan holds that death, as Qur’anic teaching presents it, is transition from one mode of life to another; even in ordinary usage as the privation of life, it has an existential aspect and can be called created. Creating life and death is a test that distinguishes the best in deeds and therefore entails subsequent recompense. The intended end is the goodness of that recompense: good-doers are the primary intended objects, while others are intended for their sake. Al-Mizan argues that human beings normally acquire either virtue or its contrary, since al-fiṭrah would lead to good were evil not presented; as a tree is directed toward fruit, virtuous deeds are directed beyond themselves to an unblemished paradisal life. God is al-ʿAzīz, whom none can overcome and who calls opponents to account, and al-Ghafūr, who pardons much in this world and hereafter. The two names unite warning and hope, and the verse introduces the proof that resurrection is necessary for recompense.
verses.3: Al-Mizan reads the seven heavens as mutually congruous and layered. Negating al-tafāwut means that creation contains no departure from wisdom: its parts are joined in a management in which their goals and benefits cooperate, even where causes seem to conflict, like the opposed pans of a scale serving its operator’s purpose. The possessive phrase “creation of the Most Merciful” indicates that generic mercy is creation’s aim. Repeated looking means careful, minute scrutiny, which will find no fuṭūr—deficiency, weakness, or disorder.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that karratayn, though dual in form, intensifies repeated return of the gaze. After such scrutiny, sight returns humbled, constricted, and defeated, and exhausted either by its own effort or by fatigue imposed on it, because it finds no imperfection. Together with the preceding verse, this establishes the universe as one united system whose parts are bound together.
verses.5: Al-Mizan identifies the lamps adorning the lower heaven as stars and understands their use as rujūm to mean that eavesdropping satans are pelted, while the wicked jinn are prepared for the burning chastisement. It reports that al-kawākib can include both fixed stars and shooting stars; on one account, shooting stars split from the fixed stars and serve as the missiles, whereas the fixed bodies depart only when God wills their destruction. The commentary judges this account the closest to contemporary scientific views.
verses.6: Al-Mizan presents this as the chapter’s threat following proofs of lordship. Disbelief in the Lord embraces not only polytheists who assign universal lordship to lesser deities, or those who deny it outright, but also those who affirm God while separating Him from His messengers. The verse reconnects to (67:2), confirming resurrection and recompense after the test of life and death.
verses.7: Al-Mizan explains shahīq as a prolonged drawing in of breath, so that hell draws the disbelievers inward as the chest draws air. As it boils and seethes (fawarān), it raises and drops them and almost breaks apart (tamayyuz) from its intense rage (ghayẓ).
verses.8: Al-Mizan says the disbelievers enter hell in rushing groups (fawj), so followers are joined to those they followed in deviation. Its khazanah are the angels charged with administering its differing punishments. Each group is then rebuked by these guardians: did a warner-prophet not come to them?
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads the inmates’ answer as their confession that a warner came but they rejected him, denied revelation, and declared him greatly astray. It rejects as contextually remote the alternatives that the final declaration is the angels’ reply or the messengers’ words reported by the angels.
verses.10: Al-Mizan takes hearing (al-samʿ) here to mean heeding a messenger’s trustworthy counsel and acting on what it requires, not merely perceiving speech. Pondering (al-ʿaql) distinguishes good from evil and benefit from harm, and here means complying with the truth known by rational consideration. Hearing is mentioned first because the general public chiefly benefits from it, whereas the few elite benefit from intellectual penetration. Thus the inmates of the Fire admit that, had they obeyed the messengers or reflected on the truth that required submission, they would not have remained among the Fire’s inhabitants. The commentary adds that moral responsibility rests on evidences acquired through listening and pondering.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says the disbelievers’ confession follows their regret over neglected duty and lost good: they admit deeds whose consequence was entry into hell, and hence their dhanb. The singular has the force of the verbal noun (al-maṣdar), while al-suḥq, the crumbling or removal mentioned at the close, is an imprecation against them. The next verse completes the contrast: believers who fear their Lord behind the veils of the unseen receive forgiveness and a great reward; fear is singled out because the context is warning.
verses.12: Al-Mizan says the disbelievers’ confession follows their regret over neglected duty and lost good: they admit deeds whose consequence was entry into hell, and hence their dhanb. The singular has the force of the verbal noun (al-maṣdar), while al-suḥq, the crumbling or removal mentioned at the close, is an imprecation against them. The next verse completes the contrast: believers who fear their Lord behind the veils of the unseen receive forgiveness and a great reward; fear is singled out because the context is warning.
verses.13: Al-Mizan treats the verse as removing the objection that, although God’s kingdom, power, creation, and governance have been demonstrated, resurrection and recompense would require knowledge encompassing human states and deeds. People may judge innumerable outward and inward acts uncountable by measuring God against their own incapacity. The verse refutes this: concealed and spoken words are alike to God, and their mention illustrates that hidden and manifest deeds alike fall within His cognizance.
verses.14: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as a rebuke to the thought that God cannot accurately reckon the multitude of human deeds. God knows all apparent and hidden deeds because He creates the realities of things and determines, connects, and conveys their effects. Voluntary human acts are attributed to their doers, yet God creates them through their free choice and all relevant causes. Since a creator is also attributed the effects necessary to a subject’s existence, human states and deeds cannot lie outside creation; otherwise this proof from creation to knowledge would fail. The two divine names at the close express His penetrating awareness of the inward particulars of beings and their effects.
verses.15: Al-Mizan explains zalūlan as what is easy to ride or use without resistance, and manākib, literally shoulder joints, as a figure for the earth’s surface. The earth’s docility denotes its subjection to human settlement, movement, and activity; eating its provision is permissive and entails seeking it by action. Al-nushūr means revivifying the dead, and the return to God makes Him alone the ruler of resurrection, reckoning, and recompense, just as He manages worldly life by stabilizing the earth and provisioning people. The imagery also, the commentary says, plainly hints at the earth as a moving spherical planet.
verses.16: Al-Mizan presents this as a warning after the proof of lordship, rebuking those who ignore their Lord’s blessings and invent peers for Him. “He who is in heaven” apparently denotes the angels entrusted with cosmic events: by God’s permission they could split the earth and make the rejecters disappear into it as it rolls and quakes (al-mawr). The commentary records the reading that it denotes God’s power, authority, and command in heaven, which avoids locating God in space, but judges it contrary to the apparent sense.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains al-ḥāṣib as a wind bearing pebbles and stones, such as the storm sent upon Lot’s people. The warning consequently challenges those secure in rejecting divine lordship: they will learn the reality of God’s indhār when such punishment comes. It rejects as absurd the view that al-nadhīr here is an adjective meaning the Prophet as warner rather than the verbal noun “warning.”
verses.18: Al-Mizan treats the fate of earlier deniers as confirmation of the prior threat. Nakīr may mean punishment and the alteration of blessings, or denial expressed by destroying and eradicating them; either way, it makes God’s disapproval terrible. The shift from direct address to “those before them” lowers the present disbelievers’ standing: their failure to reflect on lordship and fear divine displeasure renders them unworthy of direct address, so the Prophet is addressed to convey the warning.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains ṣāffāt as birds’ wings spread in flight and yaqbiḍna as their contraction; the collective al-ṭayr takes plural forms because it denotes the class of birds. Their being held aloft is a sign of God’s unity in lordship: even where natural causes operate, those causes terminate in God. Phenomena whose proximate causes are initially hidden make this especially apparent; once such causes are learned, reason must still seek their cause until it reaches God. Al-Zamakhsharī’s reported grammatical explanation makes spread wings the normal basis of flight and contraction incidental, hence the participle for the former and verb for the latter. Al-Mizan also allows that not falling while wings are spread and not falling while they contract are two signs. Following the earth’s docility, the image displays divine grace, favor, and mercy.
verses.20: Al-Mizan says the direct address intensifies the rebuke of people who take other creatures as deities to aid them. None besides the Merciful can help if He wills evil or punishment, for their supposed helpers are themselves His owned creatures and cannot benefit or harm themselves or others. Their inability to answer exposes the deception that has made them take their alleged gods for gods.
verses.21: Al-Mizan asks who could replace God by feeding people if He withheld provision. The truth is already manifest, yet the disbelievers refuse belief, assent, and obedience; they persistently turn away from it with disdain and aversion.
verses.22: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical comparison as censure of likening two unequal conditions. The importunate disbeliever, stubbornly arrogant and averse to truth despite knowing it, is like one who walks prone upon his face: unable to see rises, hollows, or his destination. The believer seeking truth walks upright on a straight path, sees where he steps and what lies ahead, and is safe from destruction. The verse is therefore a general parable of the persistent ignorant disbeliever and the discerning believer.
verses.23: Al-Mizan defines al-inshāʾ as origination from inception without a prior material model. The transformation of material stages into a conscious, hearing, seeing human being by addition of the soul is such a new creation, unlike the preceding material changes. God’s making ears, eyes, and hearts is likewise creative making: hearing and sight stand for the apparent senses generally, while the heart is the reflective, intelligent soul. Thus people are distinguished from inanimate and plant life by their special creation and senses, and from animals by intellect. The verse reproves their little gratitude for these supreme blessings.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains dharʾ as creation and reads humanity’s multiplication on earth as an attachment to its material life and adornments. These make earthly perfection dependent on deeds amid a test that distinguishes virtuous from vicious people. Gathering to God then denotes the decisive promise of resurrection and recompense.
verses.25: Al-Mizan identifies “this threat” as the promised resurrection and gathering, which the disbelievers mockingly demand be hastened.
verses.26: Al-Mizan reads the reply as saying that only God knows the time of resurrection and gathering, while the Prophet’s office is solely to give clear warning that they will occur. In this contextual reading, al-ʿilm means the particular knowledge of their time. It also allows the generic reading: all knowledge belongs to God and can be grasped only by His permission; He has not granted the Prophet knowledge of when resurrection comes, only of its certainty and his duty to warn.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains al-zulfah as imminent nearness, and takes “it” as the threatened event, though punishment is also suggested. When it is immediately before the deniers, defeat and loss appear on their sorrowful faces. “What you used to call for” means the threat they demanded be hastened by asking when it would come. The apparent context makes angels, by God’s command, the speakers, though it is also said that disbelievers may say it to one another.
verses.28: Al-Mizan has the Prophet ask the disbelievers whether God’s destroying him and the believers or mercifully sparing them could protect the disbelievers from the painful punishment their disbelief has made certain. The fate of the Prophet and his followers therefore does them no good. It reports that Meccan disbelievers prayed for their destruction; the instructed reply is that the believers’ affair rests with God and they hope in His mercy, whereas their opponents still have no protector from punishment.
verses.29: Al-Mizan says the One whose unity the Prophet calls them to, and whom they invoke against him, is the Merciful whose blessings pervade all things. The believers have faith in Him and rely exclusively on Him, not on people or wealth. Citing al-Kashshāf, the commentary explains the order of the objects: belief is phrased to expose the disbelievers’ disbelief, while the fronted object in reliance stresses exclusive trust in God. The parties will then know which is plainly astray.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains al-ghawr as water’s sinking and seeping away, and maʿīn as visible, flowing water: none can restore it if God removes it. It reports applications of the verse to the wilāyah of Imām ʿAlī and his opponents, but classifies them as al-jary—the application of a meaning to possible instances—not tafsīr of the verse.
